kurals.tamil:
சூழ்ச்சி முடிவு துணிவெய்தல் அத்துணிவு
தாழ்ச்சியுள் தங்குதல் தீது.
kurals.transliteration:
Soozhchi mudivu thunivu eydhal aththunivu
Thaazhchiyul thangudhal theedhu.
kurals.meaning: The purpose of deliberation is to arrive at a firm decision; once that decision is reached, letting it sit idle in delay is a harm.
kurals.elementary: Imagine your team spends all of recess deciding which game to play, finally agrees on tag, and then just stands around until the bell rings. All that planning was wasted. This kural says: think carefully, decide, and then actually start.
kurals.university: The chapter opens by linking it to the preceding chapters on counsel (soozhchi, deliberation) and firmness in action (vinaith thitpam, ch. 67): the telos (mudivu) of counsel is thunivu, a settled resolve, not endless discussion. Thaazhchi means lowering, lagging or delay, and thangudhal 'to remain, to linger', so the second line pictures a resolve that has sunk into procrastination; theedhu (evil, harm) ranks such delay as a positive fault rather than mere inefficiency. Parimelazhagar glosses the kural as teaching that once the ministers' counsel has concluded in a decision, the king must not let time pass before execution, because delay lets circumstances and the enemy change. Older editions print the couplet with full sandhi (துணிவெய்த லத்துணிவு / தாழ்ச்சியுட் டங்குத றீது), as in thirukkural-thamizh.org, but the words are identical. The maxim closely matches the proverb Aristotle cites in Nicomachean Ethics VI.9: deliberate slowly, execute quickly.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Arjun said: O Infallible One, by Your grace my illusion has been dispelled, and I am situated in knowledge. I am now free from doubts, and I shall act according to Your instructions.”
hinduism.explanation: After eighteen chapters of dialogue, Arjuna announces that his doubts are gone and he will now act, which ends the counsel and begins the battle.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita's long deliberation ends exactly as the Kural prescribes: in a doubt-free resolve (thunivu) that is carried straight into action.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong structural match of counsel ending in resolve and action; the Gita's frame is spiritual surrender rather than statecraft.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And Jesus said unto him, No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.”
christianity.explanation: A would-be follower asks to delay his commitment to say goodbye at home, and Jesus answers that someone who starts ploughing and keeps looking back is not ready.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts treat hesitation after a decision has been made as a real failure, not a harmless pause.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on the fault of delaying a commitment; Luke's context is discipleship rather than executing a policy decision.

islam.quote_or_event: “So pardon them and ask forgiveness for them and consult them in the matter. And when you have decided, then rely upon Allāh.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet is told to consult his companions, and once he has made up his mind, to put his trust in God and proceed.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's sequence exactly: consultation (soozhchi), then resolve (azm, thunivu), then action without wavering.
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on the consult-decide-act sequence; the Quran adds reliance on God, which the Kural leaves implicit.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Say not: ‘when I shall have leisure I shall study;’ perhaps you will not have leisure.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel warns against postponing a good resolution to some later, more convenient time, because that time may never come.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Hillel treats a resolve that is left to wait for later as a resolve that will likely fail.
judaism._accuracy_note: Clear warning against procrastination after deciding; Hillel speaks of Torah study, not affairs of state.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hasten to do good; restrain your mind from evil. He who is slow in doing good, his mind delights in evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha urges quick action on good intentions, because slowness gives the mind room to slide back into bad habits.
buddhism.tie_back: The Dhammapada and the Kural agree that delay after a good decision is not neutral; it actively opens the way to harm.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on the harm of slowness; the Buddhist focus is moral purification rather than executing a counselled plan.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod tells his brother Perses not to put off work until tomorrow or the day after, because a man who delays never fills his barn and is always wrestling with ruin.
greek_mythology.explanation: In his farming poem Hesiod treats postponement as the main enemy of the careful farmer, who must act as soon as the work is due.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod's delaying farmer who wrestles with ruin is the Kural's theedhu: a decision left idle turns into damage.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; Hesiod warns against delay in general and does not frame it as the end of deliberation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “They say that one should carry out quickly the conclusions of one's deliberation, but should deliberate slowly.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle, discussing excellence in deliberation, cites the common saying that thinking should be slow but carrying out the result should be fast.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost a Greek translation of Kural 671: counsel is meant to end in resolve, and resolve should not lag.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VI.9 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close match; Aristotle reports the maxim rather than arguing for it at length.

kurals.tamil:
தூங்குக தூங்கிச் செயற்பால தூங்கற்க
தூங்காது செய்யும் வினை.
kurals.transliteration:
Thoonguga thoongich cheyarpaala thoongarka
Thoongaadhu seyyum vinai.
kurals.meaning: Take your time over tasks that are best done slowly, but never delay tasks that must be done at once.
kurals.elementary: Planting a tree is something you can take your time over, choosing the best spot. But if the bathtub is overflowing, you turn off the tap right now. A wise person knows which jobs can wait and which cannot.
kurals.university: The couplet is a famous piece of verbal play: the verb thoongu appears five times, in the sense of 'to delay, to be slow, to tarry' (literally to droop or hang, and by extension to sleep). Parimelazhagar explains that some undertakings (such as those whose moment has not yet come) are properly done by waiting, while others (such as those where the opportunity or the enemy will not wait) must be done without any delay; the skill lies in telling the two apart. The kural therefore qualifies 671: the rule is not simply 'hurry' but correct timing, echoing the earlier chapter on knowing the right time (kaalam aridhal, ch. 49). Modern commentators Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it the same way, and there are no significant textual variants. It pairs naturally with the Latin-Greek motto festina lente and with Francis Bacon's essay on delays.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Gautama orders his son Chirakari (the slow-acting one) to kill his mother in anger; Chirakari, by nature deliberate, weighs the command at length, and by the time he has finished Gautama has repented and rejoices that his son was slow.
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma tells this story to show that in grave, irreversible matters, slowness can be the wise course.
hinduism.tie_back: Chirakari's story illustrates the first half of the Kural, that some deeds are rightly slept over, while Bhishma's wider teaching insists that urgent duties must not be delayed.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, the story of Chirakari (Ganguli trans., Santi Parva section 266)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong illustration of praiseworthy delay; covers only the first half of the Kural's two-sided rule.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.”
christianity.explanation: James tells believers that some responses should be quick and others slow.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, James does not praise speed or slowness in themselves; he assigns each to the right kind of act.
christianity._accuracy_note: Same two-speed structure; James applies it to speech and anger rather than to undertakings.

islam.quote_or_event: “There is hesitation in everything except in the actions of the next world.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that careful, unhurried deliberateness (tu'ada) is good in most matters, but deeds that serve the hereafter should be done promptly.
islam.tie_back: The hadith draws exactly the Kural's line between tasks that may wait and tasks that must not.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 4810 (graded sahih by al-Albani)
islam._accuracy_note: Close structural match; the hadith sorts tasks by worldly versus religious, while the Kural sorts them by urgency.

judaism.quote_or_event: “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet opens his famous poem by saying that each activity has its own proper time.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's two-speed rule depends on this same idea: each task has its right time, fast or slow.
judaism._accuracy_note: General principle of right timing; Kohelet does not explicitly contrast what may wait with what may not.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha explains that even when he has something true and beneficial to say, he waits for the proper time to say it, choosing the moment with care.
buddhism.explanation: In the Abhaya Sutta the Buddha describes his speech as governed by a sense of the right time as well as by truth and benefit.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Buddha treats timing as part of doing an act well: some things are best held back until their moment.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; addresses timing of speech, not a general rule about which tasks must be hurried.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The emperor Augustus often repeated the Greek saying speude bradeos, hasten slowly, and held that whatever is done well enough is done quickly enough.
greek_mythology.explanation: Suetonius reports that Augustus disliked rashness in a commander and liked this paradoxical motto.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hasten slowly captures the Kural's balance: urgency where needed, patience where haste would spoil the work.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Greek-Roman proverb rather than myth; it compresses both speeds into one motto instead of sorting tasks.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Francis Bacon advises that the beginnings of great actions be entrusted to Argus with his hundred eyes, and their ends to Briareus with his hundred hands: watch patiently first, then act swiftly.
philosophy.explanation: In his essay on delays Bacon argues that there is a ripe moment for every action, to be waited for patiently and then seized at once.
philosophy.tie_back: Bacon's two giants stand for the two halves of the Kural: slowness where waiting helps, speed where it does not.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; very close in substance to the Kural's teaching on timing.

kurals.tamil:
ஒல்லும்வா யெல்லாம் வினைநன்றே ஒல்லாக்கால்
செல்லும்வாய் நோக்கிச் செயல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ollumvaai ellaam vinai nandre ollaakkaal
Sellumvaai nokkich cheyal.
kurals.meaning: Wherever direct action is possible it is best to take it; where it is not, look for a route that will work and proceed that way.
kurals.elementary: If the front door is open, you walk straight in. If it is locked, you don't give up; you go round to the back door or ask someone for the key. Pick the way that actually works.
kurals.university: Ollum vaai means 'where it is possible (feasible)', and sellum vaai 'the way that will go through, the effective route'. Parimelazhagar reads vinai here in its political sense of open action against an enemy, that is, danda (force), the last of the four classical expedients (sama, dana, bheda, danda); where force can succeed it is best, and where it cannot one must choose among the remaining expedients. Solomon Pappaiah follows this reading explicitly, while Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the couplet more generally as 'do the work directly where you can, otherwise find a workable way'. The older sandhi text reads வினைநன்றே யொல்லாக்காற் with no difference of meaning. The teaching is pragmatic flexibility of means within a fixed end, a theme shared with the Arthashastra and later Machiavelli.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Manu teaches that among the four expedients, conciliation, gifts, division and force, the wise commend conciliation and force for the prosperity of a kingdom, choosing the means that suit the situation.
hinduism.explanation: The law code gives the king a menu of methods and expects him to pick whichever will actually work.
hinduism.tie_back: Parimelazhagar reads this Kural within the same fourfold scheme of upayas: use force where it can succeed, otherwise another means.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; same classical framework the commentator uses, though Manu does not state the if-not-then-another rule in one line.

christianity.quote_or_event: “To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak: I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes changing his approach for each audience so that his mission succeeds by whatever route is open.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts hold the goal fixed and treat the method as flexible, choosing whatever way will get through.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on flexible means; Paul's context is evangelism, not political action.

islam.quote_or_event: “So, if I forbid you to do something, then keep away from it. And if I order you to do something, then do of it as much as you can.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet ties duty to capacity: do what is possible, to the extent it is possible.
islam.tie_back: The hadith shares the Kural's ollum vaai logic: act fully wherever you are able.
islam._accuracy_note: Captures the first half (act where possible); it does not address switching to another method.

judaism.quote_or_event: Before meeting his estranged brother Esau, Jacob prepares on three fronts at once: a gift to appease him, prayer to God, and a plan for battle, dividing his camp so that one part could escape.
judaism.explanation: Rashi draws from the verses that Jacob readied himself for gifts, prayer and war, so that if one means failed another would be at hand.
judaism.tie_back: Jacob embodies the Kural's teaching: prepare the direct way, and have other workable routes ready when it will not serve.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a strong narrative example of layered means, drawn from Rashi's reading rather than the plain verse alone.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the parable of the burning house, a father cannot get his playing children out by simply calling them, so he promises them wonderful carts outside, and they run out to safety.
buddhism.explanation: The Lotus Sutra uses this story to explain upaya, skilful means: when the direct way fails, a teacher finds another route that works.
buddhism.tie_back: The father does exactly what the Kural says: when the direct approach is not possible, look for the way that gets through.
buddhism.source: Lotus Sutra, chapter 3 (parable of the burning house)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a strong match on switching methods, set in a religious rather than political frame.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After ten years of failed assaults on Troy, the Greeks, on Odysseus' plan, build the wooden horse, and the city falls by stratagem where force had not succeeded.
greek_mythology.explanation: The bard Demodocus sings of the horse at the Phaeacian court, celebrating Odysseus' cunning.
greek_mythology.tie_back: When the direct way (siege) proved impossible, the Greeks looked for the route that would get through, just as the Kural advises.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a clear case of changing means, though the ruse is ethically more doubtful than anything the Kural endorses.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli says a prince must know how to fight both by law and by force, and must imitate both the lion and the fox, since the lion cannot avoid traps and the fox cannot drive off wolves.
philosophy.explanation: He argues that a ruler needs more than one way of acting and must switch according to what the situation allows.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise holds that where one means (force) will not work, the wise agent turns to another.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; similar flexibility of means, but Machiavelli openly allows deceit, which the Kural (see ch. 66 on pure action) does not.

kurals.tamil:
வினைபகை என்றிரண்டின் எச்சம் நினையுங்கால்
தீயெச்சம் போலத் தெறும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vinai pagai endru irandin echcham ninaiyungaal
Theeyechcham polath therum.
kurals.meaning: Think it through: an unfinished task and an enemy only partly dealt with are like the embers of a fire left burning, which grow back and destroy.
kurals.elementary: When you put out a campfire, you pour water until every last glowing coal is out, because one hidden ember can start a big fire later. A job left half-done, or a quarrel only half-settled, is like that ember.
kurals.university: Echcham means 'remainder, leftover', and theeyechcham 'the remnant of a fire'; therum means 'will burn, will destroy'. Parimelazhagar notes that an unfinished undertaking and a partly subdued enemy both look small and harmless, but grow unnoticed, like smouldering embers, until they destroy the one who neglected them; Mu. Varadarasanar stresses this unseen growth. The thought is a commonplace of Indian niti: the Mahabharata's counsel of Kanika (Shanti Parva 12.138.58, critical edition) lists the remnant of a debt, of a fire and of an enemy as things that grow again and again if left unchecked. The older sandhi text reads வினைபகை யென்றிரண்டி னெச்ச நினையுங்காற் / றீயெச்சம் with no change in meaning. Modern readers often apply the enemy half to unresolved conflicts or problems rather than literal foes.

hinduism.explanation: In this Sanskrit verse, Kanika tells King Shatrumtapa that what is left over of a debt, a fire or an enemy, however small, grows again and again if it is not dealt with.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the same image and the same pairing as the Kural: a leftover fire and a leftover enemy both come back to destroy.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one parallel, including the fire image; the Sanskrit adds debt, and the Kural adds the unfinished task.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish it, all that behold it begin to mock him, Saying, This man began to build, and was not able to finish.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus describes a builder who starts a tower without the means to complete it and ends up a laughing stock.
christianity.tie_back: Luke shows the cost of the first half of the Kural's warning: an unfinished task does not stay harmless but turns against the one who left it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on the harm of unfinished work; Luke stresses shame, not the growing danger captured by the fire image.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet is reported to have said that God loves it when any of you does a piece of work, that you do it with itqan, that is, thoroughly and completely.
islam.explanation: This hadith makes finishing and perfecting a task a quality God loves.
islam.tie_back: It supports the task half of the Kural: work should be taken to completion, not left in pieces.
islam.source: Hadith in al-Bayhaqi, Shu'ab al-Iman (graded hasan by al-Albani, al-Silsila al-Sahiha 1113)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from a secondary source; covers thorough completion but not the enemy half or the danger of remnants.

judaism.quote_or_event: King Saul is commanded to finish the war with Amalek but spares King Agag and the best of the spoil; Samuel tells him that because of this incomplete obedience the kingdom will be torn from him.
judaism.explanation: Saul's half-finished campaign becomes the turning point of his downfall, and later tradition links the leftover Agagite line to Haman.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the story treats an enemy left partly dealt with as a smouldering danger that later consumes the one who left it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel on leaving an enemy half-finished; the biblical emphasis is on obedience to God rather than prudence.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Truly, an evil deed committed does not immediately bear fruit, like milk that does not turn sour all at once. But smoldering, it follows the fool like fire covered by ashes.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns that consequences can lie hidden like embers under ash before flaring up.
buddhism.tie_back: The same image of fire covered by ash carries the Kural's warning about remnants that look dead but are not.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong shared image; the Dhammapada speaks of karmic results of evil deeds, not unfinished tasks or enemies.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Heracles cuts off the heads of the Lernaean Hydra, two grow back for each one; only when Iolaus burns each stump with firebrands can the monster be finished off.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Hydra shows that an enemy only partly destroyed regrows stronger unless the job is completed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Hydra's regrowing heads are the Kural's echcham: a remnant that multiplies unless it is fully dealt with.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a vivid match for the enemy half, with fire again as the means of completion.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli advises that if an injury must be done to an enemy it should be of such a kind that there is no fear of revenge, since men avenge slight injuries but cannot avenge heavy ones.
philosophy.explanation: He argues that half-measures against opponents are the worst policy because they provoke without disabling.
philosophy.tie_back: Machiavelli reaches the Kural's conclusion from political calculation: a half-handled enemy is a future danger.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; matches the enemy half but in a harsher ethical register than the Kural.

kurals.tamil:
பொருள்கருவி காலம் வினையிடனொடு ஐந்தும்
இருள்தீர எண்ணிச் செயல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Porul karuvi kaalam vinai idanodu aindhum
Irul theera ennich cheyal.
kurals.meaning: Before acting, think through five things (resources, instruments, time, the nature of the task and place) until no confusion about them remains.
kurals.elementary: Before baking a cake you check: Do I have the ingredients? Do I have a bowl and an oven? Do I have enough time before dinner? Do I know the recipe? Is the kitchen free? Once all five are clear, you start.
kurals.university: The kural lists five factors: porul (wealth, resources), karuvi (instruments, which Parimelazhagar extends to the army and other means), kaalam (time), vinai (the nature and method of the act itself) and idam (place). Irul theera, 'until the darkness is dispelled', means until every doubt has been removed. Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah add that each factor must be weighed for both oneself and the enemy, so this is a comparative strategic appraisal and not just a checklist. The structure closely matches the Arthashastra's five limbs of counsel (1.15), which include means, men and materials, and the apportionment of place and time, and it summarises earlier Kural chapters on strength (48), time (49) and place (50). Older editions print the line with full sandhi (வினையிடனொ டைந்து / மிருடீர வெண்ணிச் செயல்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya lists five limbs of counsel: the means of starting an undertaking, the excellence of men and materials, the allotment of place and time, remedies against failure, and the successful completion of the work.
hinduism.explanation: The Arthashastra makes these five points the required agenda of any royal council before an undertaking.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts insist on a fixed five-part review, with resources, instruments, place and time at its core, before any action is begun.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a very close structural parallel, though the two lists of five overlap only partly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “If the iron be blunt, and he do not whet the edge, then must he put to more strength: but wisdom is profitable to direct.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher observes that working with a blunt tool wastes effort, and wisdom lies in preparing the instrument first.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's karuvi point: examining your instruments beforehand is part of acting wisely.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches one of the five factors (instruments) well; does not address resources, time or place.

islam.quote_or_event: “And prepare against them whatever you are able of power and of steeds of war by which you may terrify the enemy of Allah and your enemy.”
islam.explanation: The Quran instructs the community to prepare material strength and means before any confrontation.
islam.tie_back: It asks for the same preparation of resources and instruments that the Kural's first two factors describe.
islam._accuracy_note: Clear call to prepare means and instruments; lacks the Kural's explicit attention to time, place and the nature of the task.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rebuilding Jerusalem's wall under threat, Nehemiah has the builders work with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other, posts guards at the exposed places, and sets working hours from dawn until the stars appear.
judaism.explanation: Nehemiah plans resources, tools, place and time together so the work can be finished despite enemies.
judaism.tie_back: His careful planning of means, instruments, time and place is a working example of the Kural's five-fold review.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a narrative example rather than a stated principle, but it covers most of the five factors.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha lists five wrong times for striving (old age, illness, famine, danger and a split in the community) and five right times when conditions support effort.
buddhism.explanation: In the Samaya Sutta he teaches that the success of practice depends on choosing favourable times and conditions.
buddhism.tie_back: This reflects the Kural's kaalam factor: an act must be weighed against the time and conditions in which it is attempted.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; covers the time factor only, and in a spiritual rather than practical context.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Calypso gives Odysseus a bronze axe, an adze and augers, shows him where the tall dry trees stand, and brings sailcloth; he builds his raft in four days and sets out on the fifth with a fair wind she sends.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus' escape succeeds because materials, tools, place, craft and timing all come together before he sails.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The episode is almost a story version of the Kural's five factors: resources, instruments, time, the work itself and place.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a good narrative fit, though Homer presents it as divine help rather than a stated method.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle lists the circumstances of an action: who acts, what is done, about what or in what it is done, sometimes with what instrument, for what end, and how.
philosophy.explanation: He sets out these particulars to show what a person must know for an act to be truly voluntary and deliberate.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Aristotle breaks action into a fixed set of circumstances, including instrument, manner and setting, all of which must be clear before acting well.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a similar analytical list, though Aristotle's purpose is moral responsibility rather than practical planning.

kurals.tamil:
முடிவும் இடையூறும் முற்றியாங்கு எய்தும்
படுபயனும் பார்த்துச் செயல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Mudivum idaiyoorum mutriyaangu eydhum
Padupayanum paarththuch cheyal.
kurals.meaning: Act only after weighing the effort needed to finish the task, the obstacles that may arise on the way, and the great gain it will bring once completed.
kurals.elementary: Before starting a big jigsaw puzzle, ask: How long will it take to finish? What could go wrong, like the cat scattering pieces? And will the finished picture be worth it? If yes, begin.
kurals.university: Mudivu here is read by Parimelazhagar as the effort (muyarchi) required to bring the work to completion, idaiyooru as the hindrances that may come in between, and padupayan as the large yield obtained when it is completed (mutriyaangu eydhum). The kural thus sets out a three-part cost-benefit appraisal: cost of completion, risk, and return. Mu. Varadarasanar reads mudivu more simply as 'the way of completing the task', while Kalaignar reorders the three items but keeps the sense. The older sandhi text reads முடிவு மிடையூறு முற்றியாங் கெய்தும், with no difference of meaning. The idea anticipates the Gospel image of counting the cost before building, and Epictetus' advice to consider what comes before and after any undertaking.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That action is declared to be in the mode of ignorance, which is begun out of delusion, without thought to one’s own ability, and disregarding consequences, loss, and injury to others.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the lowest (tamasic) kind of action as one started without weighing consequences, loss and one's own capacity.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita condemns exactly what the Kural forbids: acting without first looking at effort, obstacles and outcome.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong inverse match; the Gita names the ignored factors (anubandha, kshaya, paurusha) that the Kural tells us to weigh.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses the image of a sensible builder who calculates whether he can complete a tower before laying its foundation.
christianity.tie_back: Counting the cost of finishing is the Kural's mudivu: weighing what completion will demand before beginning.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on the cost of completion; Luke applies it to the cost of discipleship.

islam.quote_or_event: “O Messenger of Allah! Shall I tie it and rely (upon Allah), or leave it loose and rely (upon Allah)?” He said: “Tie it and rely (upon Allah).”
islam.explanation: The Prophet tells a man to take sensible precautions against a foreseeable risk and then trust in God.
islam.tie_back: Tying the camel is guarding against the Kural's idaiyooru, the obstacles that can be foreseen and prevented before acting.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on anticipating obstacles; the hadith does not address cost of completion or expected gain.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Reckon the loss [that may be sustained through the fulfillment] of a commandment against the reward [accruing] thereby, and the gain [that may be obtained through the committing] of a transgression against the loss [entailed] thereby.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Judah the Prince teaches weighing losses against rewards before acting.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's balance of cost and padupayan (great gain), applied to moral choices.
judaism._accuracy_note: Clear cost-benefit reasoning; the Mishnah applies it to commandments and transgressions rather than practical undertakings.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells his son Rahula to reflect before any action whether it will lead to harm for himself or others, to reflect again while doing it, and again after it is done.
buddhism.explanation: Like looking in a mirror, one checks an act's results at every stage.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha, like the Kural, asks that consequences be looked at before acting rather than discovered afterwards.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the focus is moral harm rather than effort, obstacles and profit.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: A thirsty fox falls into a well; a goat jumps in after being told the water is fine; the fox climbs out on the goat's back and leaves it stranded, saying it should have looked for a way out before jumping in.
greek_mythology.explanation: Aesop's fable is traditionally summed up as look before you leap.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The goat fails to weigh the Kural's mudivu: how the venture is to be completed and brought safely to an end.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, The Fox and the Goat
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased fable rather than myth; covers foresight about completion but not gain.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In every affair consider what precedes and follows, and then undertake it. Otherwise you will begin with spirit; but not having thought of the consequences, when some of them appear you will shamefully desist.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus uses the example of the Olympic athlete, who must count the training, hardships and possible defeat before committing.
philosophy.tie_back: His advice lines up item by item with the Kural: effort to completion, obstacles along the way, and whether the gain is worth it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close match on weighing effort and obstacles before starting.

kurals.tamil:
செய்வினை செய்வான் செயன்முறை அவ்வினை
உள்ளறிவான் உள்ளம் கொளல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Seyvinai seyvaan seyanmurai avvinai
Ullarivaan ullam kolal.
kurals.meaning: The right way for anyone undertaking a task is to learn the mind of someone who knows that task from the inside.
kurals.elementary: If you want to learn to bake bread, the best first step is to ask a baker who has done it a thousand times. They know the little secrets no recipe tells you.
kurals.university: Ullarivaan means 'one who knows the inside' of the work: its hidden difficulties, tricks and secrets. Ullam kolal means 'to take (on) his mind or view'. Parimelazhagar glosses the knower as someone who has already carried out such an undertaking and knows its secret (marmam), and Solomon Pappaiah likewise reads 'one who has done this work before'. The sound pattern (seyvinai seyvaan seyanmurai; ullarivaan ullam) is deliberate and makes the couplet easy to remember. The older sandhi text reads செயன்முறை யவ்வினை / யுள்ளறிவா னுள்ளங் கொளல். The kural extends the earlier chapter on seeking the help of the great (periyaaraith thunaikkodal, ch. 45) to the practical level of expertise.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Learn the Truth by approaching a spiritual master. Inquire from him with reverence and render service unto him. Such an enlightened Saint can impart knowledge unto you because he has seen the Truth.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that real knowledge comes from someone who has seen the truth directly.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita's tattva-darshin, one who has seen the reality, is the spiritual counterpart of the Kural's ullarivaan, one who knows a task from within.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Same principle of learning from an experienced knower; the Gita concerns spiritual truth rather than a practical task.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest? And he said, How can I, except some man should guide me?”
christianity.explanation: The Ethiopian official admits he cannot understand the scripture alone and invites Philip to explain it.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, the story holds that a task is best approached by seeking out someone who understands it from inside.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on seeking an expert guide; the task here is understanding scripture.

islam.quote_or_event: “So ask the people of the message if you do not know.”
islam.explanation: The Quran tells those who lack knowledge to ask those who have it.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's method in one line: whoever does not know, should ask the one who does.
islam._accuracy_note: Close in principle; the Quranic context is knowledge of earlier revelations, though it is widely applied generally.

judaism.quote_or_event: Jethro watches Moses judging the people alone from morning to evening, tells him the method is not good and will wear him out, and advises him to appoint capable officers over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens; Moses follows the advice.
judaism.explanation: An experienced outsider who understands the work of governing shows Moses a better method.
judaism.tie_back: Moses does what the Kural recommends: he adopts the view of someone who understands how the work is best done.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a strong narrative match on taking method from an experienced adviser.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should one find a man who points out faults and who reproves, let him follow such a wise and sagacious person as one would a guide to hidden treasure.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares a wise adviser to a guide who knows where treasure is buried.
buddhism.tie_back: The guide to hidden treasure is the Kural's ullarivaan, the one who knows what is hidden inside a task.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good image of the knowing guide; the verse centres on moral correction rather than technical know-how.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Circe tells Odysseus that before he can find his way home he must go to the house of Hades and consult the seer Tiresias, who alone can tell him the route and the measure of his journey.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus makes the terrible journey because only Tiresias knows the path from within.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Even the resourceful Odysseus follows the Kural's method, seeking out the one who truly knows the task before attempting it.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; good match on consulting the knower, set in a supernatural frame.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates asks Crito whether a man in athletic training should heed the praise and blame of everyone, or only of the one man who is his doctor or trainer; Crito agrees it is the expert alone.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates uses this to argue that in any matter one should follow the person who has real knowledge of it, not the crowd.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates and the Kural agree that the proper way to act is to take the view of the one who knows the work.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a close philosophical statement of deference to expertise.

kurals.tamil:
வினையான் வினையாக்கிக் கோடல் நனைகவுள்
யானையால் யானையாத் தற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Vinaiyaan vinaiyaakkik kodal nanaikavul
Yaanaiyaal yaanaiyaath thatru.
kurals.meaning: Using one undertaking to achieve another is like using a tamed elephant in musth to capture a wild one.
kurals.elementary: When you go to the shop to buy milk and also post a letter on the way, one trip does two jobs. Long ago, people caught wild elephants by using a tame elephant to lead them in. Smart people let one job help with the next.
kurals.university: Nanaikavul, literally 'wet cheek', refers to an elephant in musth, whose temples stream with fluid; such tame elephants were used as decoys to lure and capture wild ones, a practice well attested in Tamil and Sanskrit sources on elephant-keeping. Vinaiyaan vinai aakkik kodal means 'to bring about a (further) task by means of a task'. Parimelazhagar specifies that the second undertaking should be of the same kind as the first, just as elephant catches elephant, while Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it as completing one task while doing another. The older sandhi text reads கோட னனைகவுள் / யானையால் யானையாத் தற்று. The elephant simile gives a vivid image of turning one achievement into the means of the next.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Rama helps Sugriva win back his throne from Vali, and Sugriva in return sends the monkey armies across the world to find Sita and later to build the bridge to Lanka.
hinduism.explanation: By completing one undertaking (Sugriva's restoration), Rama gains the means for his larger one (the rescue of Sita).
hinduism.tie_back: This is vinaiyaan vinai aakkik kodal on an epic scale: one completed task becomes the tool for the next.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; strong narrative fit, though the epic presents it as an alliance rather than a stated method.

christianity.quote_or_event: In the parable of the unjust steward, a manager about to lose his post uses his remaining authority over his master's accounts to win friends who will take him in later, and Jesus tells his hearers to use worldly wealth to make friends for the future.
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the shrewd steward, Jesus praises using present resources to secure a future end.
christianity.tie_back: The steward uses one piece of business to accomplish another, as the Kural's elephant is used to catch its fellow.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the thematic link (using one piece of business to secure another) is loose and the parable's moral is debated.

islam.quote_or_event: Joseph, now in charge of Egypt's grain stores, uses the distribution of grain to his visiting brothers to bring about their return with his brother Benjamin, and so to reunite his family.
islam.explanation: Surah Yusuf shows Joseph turning an administrative duty into the means of a deeper purpose.
islam.tie_back: Joseph uses one task (supplying grain) to achieve another (restoring his family), which is the Kural's method.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a fair narrative parallel, not a stated principle.

judaism.quote_or_event: “From and within the forest comes the ax to it,”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud cites this popular saying to explain why Obadiah, said to be an Edomite convert, was chosen to prophesy against Edom: the axe handle that fells the tree is cut from the forest itself.
judaism.tie_back: Like the elephant used to catch an elephant, the forest supplies the tool for its own felling: like is taken by means of like.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 39b (William Davidson trans., Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close image of like captured by like; the Talmudic context is prophecy and punishment.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that an unskilful thought can be driven out by focusing on a skilful one, as a skilled carpenter knocks out a coarse peg with a fine one.
buddhism.explanation: In the Vitakkasanthana Sutta the first method of calming the mind uses one thought to displace another.
buddhism.tie_back: The carpenter's peg, like the Kural's elephant, is a tool of the same kind used to accomplish the task.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; similar logic of like working on like, applied to meditation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Set to clean the vast Augean stables in a single day, Heracles breaches the walls and diverts the rivers Alpheus and Peneus through them, letting one force of nature do the work.
greek_mythology.explanation: Instead of doing the labour by hand, Heracles turns existing powers into his tool.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Heracles makes one thing (the rivers' flow) accomplish another (the cleansing), as the Kural's hunter uses one elephant to take another.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; good on leverage, weaker on the like-by-like aspect of the elephant image.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Francis Bacon writes that nature, to be commanded, must be obeyed: human power over nature comes from using nature's own laws and forces.
philosophy.explanation: Bacon's programme for science rests on turning natural processes against one another to achieve human ends.
philosophy.tie_back: The idea that nature is mastered by nature matches the Kural's elephant-by-elephant image.
philosophy.source: Francis Bacon, Novum Organum I, aphorism 3
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a broad philosophical echo rather than a direct parallel.

kurals.tamil:
நட்டார்க்கு நல்ல செயலின் விரைந்ததே
ஒட்டாரை ஒட்டிக் கொளல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nattaarkku nalla seyalin viraindhadhe
Ottaarai ottik kolal.
kurals.meaning: Winning over those who are not yet on your side is more urgent than doing good to those who already are your friends.
kurals.elementary: Your friends already like you. But if there is a kid in class who keeps fighting with you, making peace with them first can make everything easier for everyone. Turning a rival into a friend is the urgent job.
kurals.university: Nattaar are those already bound in friendship; ottaar are those who do not adhere to one, that is, rivals or foes, and ottik kolal is 'to make them adhere, to bring them round'. Parimelazhagar, followed by the Drew-Lazarus translation reproduced on ytamizh, specifies the foes of one's foes, so that the kural advises quickly securing allies against a common enemy before an undertaking, while modern commentators (Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) read it more broadly as reconciling enemies. Viraindhadhu, 'the more urgent', ranks this ahead of kindness to friends because friends are already secure while potential enemies can still change sides. The older sandhi text reads விரைந்ததே / யொட்டாரை யொட்டிக் கொளல். The kural fits the Indian mandala theory of alliances and also anticipates ethical teachings about turning an enemy into a friend.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Trapped between a hunter's net and hunting animals, the mouse Palita makes a timely alliance with his natural enemy, the cat Lomasa, who is caught in the net; each saves the other, and they part with prudent caution.
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira this fable to show that in need a wise king quickly makes allies even of former enemies.
hinduism.tie_back: The mouse follows the Kural exactly: bringing a foe round in time is more urgent than anything else.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, the mouse and the cat (Ganguli trans., Santi Parva section 138)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a strong strategic parallel, including the Kural's sense of urgency.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For if ye love them which love you, what thank have ye? for sinners also love those that love them. And if ye do good to them which do good to you, what thank have ye? for sinners also do even the same.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says kindness to friends is ordinary; the greater work is love toward enemies.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Luke ranks reaching out to those who are not on your side above doing good to those who already are.
christianity._accuracy_note: Same ranking of enemies over friends; Jesus' motive is love, the Kural's (in Parimelazhagar) is strategy.

islam.quote_or_event: “Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better; and thereupon the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Quran teaches that answering hostility with goodness can turn an enemy into a close friend.
islam.tie_back: This is ottaarai ottik kolal: bringing the hostile one round until he is bound to you.
islam._accuracy_note: Close match on turning enemies into friends; the Quran does not rank it against kindness to friends.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Others say: [Who is mighty?] Who turns an enemy into his friend.”
judaism.explanation: In a list of true virtues, one opinion defines real strength as making an enemy into a friend.
judaism.tie_back: The rabbis and the Kural both treat winning over a foe as a higher achievement than ordinary good deeds.
judaism.source: Avot de-Rabbi Natan 23 (trans. A. Cohen, Soncino, Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close in substance; presented as one opinion among several.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that hostility ends only through non-hostility, not by fighting it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Dhammapada gives the ethical basis for the Kural's advice to win over those who are against you.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Supports reconciliation but lacks the Kural's comparison with helping friends and its strategic edge.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Meeting on the battlefield at Troy, Glaucus and Diomedes discover that their grandfathers were guest-friends, so they refuse to fight, clasp hands and exchange armour as a pledge.
greek_mythology.explanation: Two enemies choose friendship over combat in the middle of a war.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The episode shows the Kural's ideal: turning someone on the other side into a bound friend.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; reconciliation rests on an inherited bond rather than deliberate policy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Sun Tzu holds that the best thing in war is to take the enemy's country whole and intact, and that supreme excellence is to break the enemy's resistance without fighting.
philosophy.explanation: The Art of War ranks winning an opponent over, or disarming him intact, above destroying him.
philosophy.tie_back: Sun Tzu's strategy, like the Kural's, puts bringing the adversary round ahead of other actions.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, ch. 3 (trans. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; similar strategic preference, but concerned with conquest rather than alliance.

kurals.tamil:
உறைசிறியார் உள்நடுங்கல் அஞ்சிக் குறைபெறின்
கொள்வர் பெரியார்ப் பணிந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Uraisiriyaar ulnadungal anjik kuraiperin
Kolvar periyaarp panindhu.
kurals.meaning: Rulers of a small realm, fearing the dread their own people feel, will bow to a mightier power and accept terms if an opening for peace is offered.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a small team facing a much bigger, stronger team and all your players are scared. A wise captain might agree to a fair deal instead of a hopeless match, to protect the team. Sometimes the brave choice is to make peace.
kurals.university: Uraisiriyaar, 'those whose dwelling (realm) is small', is read by Parimelazhagar as the ministers of weak states; ulnadungal anji means 'fearing the inner trembling' of their own subjects; kurai perin, 'if they obtain an opening' for reconciliation; periyaarp panindhu kolvar, 'they will submit to and embrace the great'. The Drew-Lazarus rendering on ytamizh follows this reading, while Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it more generally about the weak yielding to the strong for the sake of their people. The older sandhi text reads உண்ணடுங்க லஞ்சிக் குறைபெறிற். Placed at the end of the chapter, the kural completes the method of execution by admitting that sometimes the wise act is timely submission rather than conflict, a principle also central to the Arthashastra's teaching on the weak king and to Luke 14:31-32.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya teaches that a king who is weaker than his rival should make peace with him, and that a weak king attacked by a strong one should submit, bending like a reed, and wait for better times.
hinduism.explanation: The Arthashastra treats timely submission (samdhi) by the weaker side as sound policy, not cowardice.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's advice to the rulers of small realms: accept terms with the stronger party to protect one's people.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a very close statecraft parallel.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand? Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus describes a weaker king who, seeing he is outnumbered, sends envoys early to ask for terms.
christianity.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural's scene: a smaller ruler seeking terms from a greater one.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match; Luke uses it as an image for the cost of discipleship.

islam.quote_or_event: At al-Hudaybiyyah the Prophet accepts a truce with Quraysh on terms many of his companions found humiliating, including turning back from Mecca that year; the Quran later calls the outcome a clear victory.
islam.explanation: Accepting restrictive terms from a stronger party in the moment protected the community and opened the way to later success.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's rulers, the Prophet chose a negotiated settlement over a clash, for his people's sake.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the Muslims were not simply the weaker side submitting, so the parallel is partial.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Bring your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people, and live.”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah urges King Zedekiah to submit to Babylon's greater power rather than rebel and bring ruin on Jerusalem.
judaism.tie_back: The prophet gives the Kural's counsel to a small kingdom: bow to the greater power for the survival of the people.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match; Jeremiah grounds the advice in divine will as well as prudence.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Victory begets enmity; the defeated dwell in pain. Happily the peaceful live, discarding both victory and defeat.”
buddhism.explanation: Traditionally linked to the war between King Pasenadi and King Ajatasattu, the verse says conflict harms winner and loser alike.
buddhism.tie_back: It gives an ethical reason to prefer peace to fighting on, which supports the Kural's settlement-seeking rulers.
buddhism._accuracy_note: General preference for peace; it does not speak of the weaker side yielding to the stronger.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Old King Priam goes by night to the tent of Achilles, who has killed his son, kneels and kisses his hands, and wins back Hector's body so that Troy can mourn.
greek_mythology.explanation: The weaker king humbles himself before the stronger warrior to obtain what his people need.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Priam, like the rulers in the Kural, bows to the greater power when an opening appears, for the sake of his people.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; an emotional act of humility more than political submission.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Melian Dialogue the Athenian envoys urge the small island of Melos to yield, arguing that the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must; Melos refuses and is destroyed.
philosophy.explanation: Thucydides presents the negative case: a small state that refuses terms from a far stronger power is wiped out.
philosophy.tie_back: The fate of Melos shows, in reverse, the prudence the Kural credits to small states that bow when terms are offered.
philosophy.source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 5.84-116 (trans. Richard Crawley)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a powerful inverse parallel, though Thucydides also lets the reader question Athenian arrogance.

ytamizh-ch68.title: Thirukkural Chapter 68: வினைசெயல்வகை / Modes of Action (with Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar and Sivayogi Sivakumar commentaries)

aristotle-nicomachean.title: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, trans. W. D. Ross

abudawud-4810.title: Sunan Abi Dawud 4810 (Kitab al-Adab, chapter on gentleness)

pirkei-avot-sefaria.title: Pirkei Avot (Mishnah Avot), trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp (Mishnah Yomit)

avot-derabbi-natan.title: Avot de-Rabbi Natan, ch. 23, in The Minor Tractates of the Talmud, trans. A. Cohen (Soncino, 1965)

sanhedrin-39b.title: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 39b (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz)

mahabharata-ganguli.title: The Mahabharata, Santi Parva, trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli
